status: wave-4: pieces occupy lattice elements (volume, face, edge), not cell slots

materials.design_purpose: The first family: felled wood, worked with nothing but hands. Joinery means it can be hung and swung (doors); it cannot be cut into masonry forms or span a girder. A timber house is still a house - nothing knocks it down.

Dug from rock faces and boulders. Masonry is what the boss's stonecut mastery works with (the roof wedge and every cut form after it); heavy is a hook for later rules (a stone floor over a timber frame). It has no joinery: no stone doors.
Smelted at the forge, so a build in iron is a build that has a forge behind it. Metal spans (the girder); joinery for iron doors and hinges. Iron is not malleable: curved forms wait for bronze.

Era two's alloy (copper and tin, eras.json / D-019): the first malleable family, so it is what the arch and every curved form after it are worked from. Tough is the hook for what may carry what. It also spans and joins, so a bronze build is never worse than iron - it is iron plus curves.

shapes.design_purpose: The starting shape. Two units per block equals one harvest swing, so a small shelter visibly eats into a resource node instead of feeling free.

A thin partition standing on a vertical face of the lattice, centred on the plane the two neighbouring cells share, so it belongs to neither cell and a cube can fill either side of it. Snaps to the nearest vertical face to the crosshair - no rotation key. Half the cost of a cube so walling a shelter is cheaper than filling it.

Stands on a vertical edge of the lattice - the line where up to four walls meet - so it always lines up with the panels around it and stacks on the post below when you aim at its top. Corners where walls meet grow a post visual on their own; the placed post is for free-standing frames and for making a corner load-bearing in the player's eye.

shapes.hint: aim along a beam's line or a wall's top to run it on into the air
shapes.design_purpose: Runs along a horizontal edge of the lattice, the line a wall's top and a floor's rim share, so it reads as a lintel over a doorway, a wall plate along the top of a wall, or a rail along a slab's edge depending only on what it is next to.

shapes.hint: lies between cells: aim at the top of a wall to roof a room; for a raised floor use half cubes (G)
shapes.design_purpose: A slab lying on a horizontal face of the lattice - the plane between a cell and the one above - for floors, flat roofs and landings; available from the start because a roof is what makes a shelter (building slice 2 un-gated it; the boss reward is the pitched roof wedge instead). Same thickness as a wall so a floor's rim and a wall's top meet cleanly.

shapes.hint: R turns them; they rise toward their back
shapes.design_purpose: Two half-height steps in one cell, rising toward the back; R turns them (an oriented block, one of two shapes that use the rotation key). A cube's cost for a cube's cell, so climbing your own building is never cheaper than building it.

shapes.hint: two cells tall; E opens and shuts it, R flips the hinge; timber or iron, never stone
shapes.design_purpose: A wall piece two cells tall (the player is 1.92 m) whose leaf swings open on E and closes again; while open its collision is gone and mobs may follow you through. Occupies the face it stands on and the one above, so nothing else can straddle the opening. R flips the hinge to the other side. Costs a cube: a door is the most valuable square metre of a shelter.

shapes.unlock_hint: locked until the Forge Tyrant falls (stonecut mastery); then stone only, Q to pick it
shapes.hint: a cut stone form: stone only (Q); R turns it
shapes.design_purpose: The visible reward for the first Forge Tyrant kill (trial.json completion_unlock): a 45-degree wedge filling a cell, low at the front and full height at the back, turned with R, so pitched roofs and ramps join the vocabulary. Flat roofs from slabs are always possible; the wedge is what makes a build look finished, which is the right kind of reward - it widens what can be built without gating shelter.

shapes.hint: an iron beam two cells long: spans a room's width without a post under it
shapes.design_purpose: The first shape a material trait unlocks rather than a boss: a two-cell beam needs metal, so a forge is what widens your rooms. It occupies two edges in a row (a footprint two cells long), which is also the model any long or tall piece uses.

shapes.hint: a wall piece with a rounded opening: caps a doorway or a window; bronze or better
shapes.design_purpose: The first curved form (D-019): a wall piece whose underside is a half-round opening, so a doorway or window gets an arched head. It needs a malleable family - bronze, the era-two alloy - which is how a material's property, not a boss, unlocks a form.

Fine mode's cube: one registry cell (half a build cell each way), the same rule at half the grid. Eight of them make a cube for four times the price - detail costs, bulk is cheap - so fine pieces are for trim, steps, sills and furniture, never for walls by the metre.
Fine mode's wall: a quarter of a panel on one registry face, for parapets, window sills, half-height partitions and patching the gap a full panel cannot fit.

Fine mode's post: half a cell tall on any registry edge, including the edges through the middle of a block's top face - the owner's 'a post on a block' at sub-block scale. Balusters, table legs, fence pickets.
Fine mode's beam: half a cell long on any horizontal registry edge, for rails, sills and the small lintel over a half-wall gap.
Fine mode's slab: a quarter of a floor on one registry face, for shelves, steps between half-cubes, and roof edges.

design_purpose: grid_size_metres balances Minecraft-like constraint against detail (final value is an open question in construction.md). placement_range_metres is measured from the third-person camera, which sits about 4.5 m behind the player, so it must cover that set-back plus reach; 6 m could not reach the floor in front of the player. removal_refund_fraction controls experimentation freedom versus commitment and deliberately mirrors salvage_return_fraction in crafting.json so building and crafting feel like one economy. element (block | wall | floor | post | beam) says which kind of lattice element a shape occupies: a block takes a whole cell, a wall a vertical face shared by two cells, a floor a horizontal face, a post a vertical edge shared by four cells, a beam a horizontal edge. Placement snaps to the nearest free element of that kind to the crosshair, and two pieces only conflict when they want the same element - which is what lets a cube sit against a wall, a post stand where two walls meet, and a slab rim carry a beam, with no slot bookkeeping and no rotation key for anything but oriented shapes. lattice_divisions is how much finer the occupancy registry is than the build grid (2 = half cells): full-size pieces occupy a footprint of registry elements, which is what lets half-scale pieces (fine mode) share the world with them through one set lookup. form (box | stairs | wedge | door, default box) picks the mesh and collision the engine builds; oriented (default false) says R turns the piece; cells_tall (default 1) stacks the footprint upward, for the two-cell door. fine (default false) marks a half-scale piece that occupies one registry element, and fine_of names the full-size shape it is the fine twin of: fine mode (G) swaps the selection for its twin and back, so the palette stays nine shapes with a scale toggle rather than fourteen. materials are the building families (Q cycles the ones you carry): each is paid in its source item and carries traits; a shape may require traits (requires_traits), which is how looks and forms are gated to what a material can be worked into - joinery for doors, masonry for cut stone forms, metal for spans, and malleable reserved for the alloy family that curved forms will need. cells_long stretches a beam along its edge.
